back_blocks.md: An **alkane** is a saturated hydrocarbon with the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>. All carbon-carbon bonds in alkanes are single bonds (C-C).

cards.back_md: An **alkane** is a saturated hydrocarbon with the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>. All carbon-carbon bonds in alkanes are single bonds (C-C).

front_blocks.md: Why are alkanes described as generally unreactive compounds?

back_blocks.md: Alkanes are generally unreactive because they contain only **strong single covalent bonds** (C-C and C-H). These bonds require a lot of energy to break, making alkanes resistant to most chemical reactions.

back_blocks.md: Methane has the molecular formula **CH**<sub>**4**</sub>. It is the first alkane and follows the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> with n = 1.

front_blocks.md: What are the products of the complete combustion of an alkane?

back_blocks.md: Complete combustion of an alkane produces **carbon dioxide** and **water**. For example: CH<sub>4</sub> (g) + 2O<sub>2</sub> (g) → CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

front_blocks.md: Alkanes contain covalent bonds because they are made of non-metal atoms.

back_blocks.md: Alkanes are made entirely of carbon and hydrogen atoms, which are both **non-metals**. Non-metal atoms form **covalent bonds** by sharing electrons.

front_blocks.md: How does the boiling point change as alkane chain length increases, and why?

back_blocks.md: Boiling point **increases** with chain length. Longer alkane molecules have stronger intermolecular forces between them, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
